title: BEVSA: A Real-Time Bird's-Eye-View Semantic Segmentation Accelerator for Multi-Camera System
problem: Bird's-eye-view (BEV) semantic segmentation for multi-camera systems (MCS) requires expensive view transformation (68.3 ms on edge devices) and exhibits high input activation sparsity (69.1%), resulting in low throughput and high latency unsuitable for real-time 3D perception.
method: BEVSA is a specialized hardware accelerator with two key innovations: (1) block-decomposed hierarchical BEV pooling that partitions search space in MCS-suitable ways, achieving 43.2x speedup over edge computing for BEV transformation, and (2) coarse-to-fine-grained zero-skipping convolution that handles both channel-level and tile-level sparsity, improving convolution throughput 1.61x. Implemented at 28nm, it targets edge deployment.

title: GTN-Path: Efficient Path Timing Prediction through Waveform Propagation with Graph Transformer
problem: Static timing analysis (STA) must balance accuracy and runtime at advanced nodes; graph-based analysis (GBA) is fast but pessimistic; path-based analysis (PBA) is accurate but expensive. LUT-based standard cell libraries introduce accuracy losses vs. SPICE at advanced nodes, making sign-off STA unreliable.
method: Graph Transformer Network (GTN) that predicts post-layout path timing via waveform propagation. Models standard cells and interconnects as graphs, using transformer attention to capture structural information and propagate waveforms accurately. Predicts waveforms and delays with ~3% error vs. SPICE, achieving 3510× speedup.

title: WISEDRAM: A Reliable Bitwise In-DRAM Accelerator
problem: Processing-in-Memory (PIM) techniques in DRAM suffer from vulnerability to process variation and noise, internal cell leakage, and high latency in cell access, limiting real-world deployment of in-DRAM compute.
method: WISEDRAM uses one row of special X-cells to enable in-DRAM bulk-bitwise operations while retaining conventional DRAM cell access procedures for reliable reads/writes. This ensures reliability equivalent to standard DRAM while enabling parallel in-DRAM computation.

title: SNAPPIX: Efficient-Coding-Inspired In-Sensor Compression for Edge Vision
problem: Edge vision sensors with weak compute must transmit high-volume pixel data to remote servers, creating a severe energy bottleneck; conventional compression approaches are incompatible with task-specific requirements.
method: SNAPPIX co-designs sensor and algorithm using coded exposure (CE) as in-sensor compression strategy. It learns task-agnostic sampling patterns based on efficient coding theory, co-designs downstream vision models to handle CE pixel non-uniformity, and proposes lightweight hardware augmentations to support CE compression.

title: Weighted Range-Constrained Ising-Model Decoder for Quantum Error Correction
problem: Quantum error correction decoders must balance time complexity and error detection threshold; existing Ising-model decoders have higher complexity than union-find but inferior threshold compared to minimum-weight perfect-matching (MWPM).
method: Weighted Range-Constrained Ising (WRIM) decoder uses a polygonal region to enclose flipped syndromes, ensuring coverage of all potential error chains while optimizing Ising coupling and external field coefficients via constraint minimization.

title: OS2G: A High-Performance DPU Offloading Architecture for GPU-based Deep Learning with Object Storage
problem: Object storage for deep learning workloads imposes intensive CPU processing overhead and causes redundant data movements (DPU->host->GPU), consuming host resources and creating a data ingestion bottleneck that limits GPU utilization during training.
method: OS2G introduces a DPU offloading architecture that establishes a direct DPU-to-GPU data path, bypassing the host CPU entirely for object storage data delivery. It redesigns the object storage client to run on the DPU and exploits GPU-Direct or equivalent RDMA mechanisms to transfer data directly from the DPU's network interface into GPU memory. OS2G includes a DPU-side data processing pipeline (decompression, format conversion) to prepare DL-ready tensors before they enter GPU memory, eliminating the host CPU from the critical data path.

title: Anaheim: Architecture and Algorithms for Processing Fully Homomorphic Encryption in Memory
problem: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) workloads on GPUs are bottlenecked not by NTT (number-theoretic transform) computation but by simple element-wise modular arithmetic operations that saturate off-chip DRAM bandwidth, preventing GPUs from being practical FHE accelerators despite their computational resources.
method: Anaheim is a PIM (processing-in-memory) architecture for FHE that augments DRAM with versatile PIM units supporting modular integer arithmetic instructions (addition, multiplication, NTT butterfly, etc.) to execute element-wise operations in-memory, eliminating the off-chip bandwidth bottleneck. The design includes optimized FHE execution flows that partition computation between GPU (NTT-heavy phases) and PIM units (element-wise phases), efficient data mapping algorithms that exploit DRAM's internal structure (bank/row organization) to minimize data movement overhead within DRAM, and an end-to-end software framework for GPU-PIM co-execution.

title: A Cross-model Fusion-aware Framework for Optimizing (gather-matmul-scatter)s Workload
problem: Modern sparse and irregular neural networks (RGCN, SpConv, MoE) rely on gather-matmul-scatter workloads, but existing optimizations lack cross-model transferability, require expensive search, and cannot handle dynamic inputs efficiently.
method: Efficient-GMS proposes a fusion-aware framework with dataflow analysis to identify shared patterns and four optimized dataflow variants using vertical/horizontal fusion. A performance model predicts execution efficiency to reduce search space, and a lightweight heuristic selects optimal dataflow based on input characteristics and hardware.

title: Harrow: Synthesis of Optical Logic Circuits via Harmonic Mean and Integer Partition
problem: Photonic integrated circuits suffer from signal attenuation along light propagation paths, requiring optical-electrical conversions that introduce unwanted delays and inefficiency.
method: Harrow optimizes photonic logic synthesis from binary decision diagrams by improving the signal efficiency factor of optical combiners using harmonic mean optimization, and eliminates redundant combiners via integer partition. Techniques are arranged in an optimal operational sequence.

title: PreDAC: An Efficient Framework of Pre-Refining Enhanced Design Space Exploration for Approximate Computing
problem: Design Space Exploration (DSE) algorithms for approximate computing face challenges obtaining optimal solutions within large and complex design spaces efficiently.
method: Introduces pre-refining enhanced DSE framework that provides customized design space reduction and cost-performance formula specific to each application. Pre-refinement step reduces design space size before DSE, enabling faster convergence. Also proposes innovative cost-performance-based DSE algorithm that leverages pre-refined space.

title: EDA: Energy-Efficient Inter-Layer Model Compilation for Edge DNN Inference Acceleration
problem: Inter-layer operator scheduling on edge NPUs can reduce DRAM traffic by reusing layer outputs in on-chip SRAM, but naive deep traversal of DNN operator graphs greatly increases off-chip memory transactions when on-chip SRAM is small, negating energy savings.
method: EDA is a DNN compilation framework that first transforms the DNN model into a tensor-splitting model and decomposes the model graph into subgraphs. An inter-layer cost model rapidly determines the optimal operator traversal depth for each subgraph given the available on-chip SRAM. EDA then manages the on-chip shared memory space to prevent overflow, and applies operator grouping to improve MAC unit and SRAM space utilization. The resulting compilation avoids both excessive DRAM traffic (from too-deep traversal) and under-utilization (from too-shallow traversal).

title: Veritas - Demystifying Silent Data Corruptions: uArch-Level Modeling and Fleet Data of Modern x86 CPUs
problem: Silent Data Corruptions (SDCs) caused by silicon defects in arithmetic units (integer and FP units) of modern x86 CPUs are poorly characterized at the microarchitecture level; no public data exists on SDC incident rates across CPU microarchitectures or workloads at fleet scale.
method: A full-system gem5-based fault injector models hardware faults in arithmetic units (integer and floating-point) of five modern x86 microarchitectures. Fault injection experiments measure SDC probability and rates across arithmetic unit types and instruction classes. Real-world defect rate data from large-scale datacenter experiments is integrated with the simulation model to estimate SDC incident rates in deployed fleets.

title: ZenLeak: Practical Last-Level Cache Side-Channel Attacks on AMD Zen Processors
problem: AMD's non-inclusive caches have been assumed resistant to LLC side-channel attacks due to reverse-engineering challenges; practical attack feasibility on Zen processors remains undemonstrated.
method: ZenLeak reverse-engineers AMD's cache addressing for L2 set index, L3 slice, and L3 set index; constructs eviction sets for non-inclusive caches by solving eviction patterns; demonstrates first LLC side-channel attack on AMD Zen CPUs via OpenSSL AES T-table.

title: In-Memory Arithmetic: Enabling Division with Stochastic Logic
problem: Efficient hardware division has been a long-standing challenge; traditional binary approaches require multiple cycles and complex control logic. Emerging in-memory computing faces additional obstacles: noise sensitivity, process variation, and the inherent difficulty of binary operations in noisy substrates.
method: The approach uses stochastic computing (SC) to implement division within an MTJ-based in-memory architecture; SC represents numbers as bitstreams and performs arithmetic through simple logic operations, naturally tolerating noise. MTJ memory provides the substrate for logic-in-memory operations, reducing the data movement penalty.

title: Hybe: GPU-NPU Hybrid System for Efficient LLM Inference with Million-Token Context Window
problem: LLM inference with million-token context windows is infeasible on GPUs alone because KV cache activation memory for long contexts (>100K tokens) exceeds total GPU DRAM capacity, making batching impractical and leaving GPU compute cores severely underutilized during the memory-bandwidth-bound decode stage. The compute-memory imbalance between compute-intensive prefill and memory-intensive decode cannot be addressed by batching when KV data dominates physical memory.
method: Hybe assigns the compute-intensive prefill stage to existing high-throughput GPUs (NVIDIA H100 with vLLM) and offloads the memory-bandwidth-bound decode stage to lightweight NPUs sized with exactly enough compute to saturate their HBM bandwidth. The key mechanism is fine-grained KV transmission: as the GPU produces partial KV activations during prefill, it immediately streams them to NPU HBM over interconnect, reducing peak GPU memory footprint dramatically. A stage-wise pipeline scheduler dynamically assigns incoming requests to idle GPU or NPU hardware, minimizing pipeline stalls across the two-stage heterogeneous system. Hybe NPU is implemented in 4nm process with HBM matching the H100 HBM specification.

title: AccelES: Accelerating Top-K SpMV for Embedding Similarity via Low-bit Pruning
problem: Top-K sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) for recommendation system embedding similarity suffers from high latency due to inefficient memory access patterns when scanning full-precision sparse matrices to identify the most relevant embeddings.
method: AccelES employs a two-stage computation scheme: Stage 1 uses a compact low-bit (pruned) representation of the sparse matrix to rapidly identify the top-K candidate entries with minimal data movement, and Stage 2 performs full-precision SpMV only on this pruned candidate subset. Two novel sparse matrix storage formats, Ultra-CSR and Random-CSR, are introduced to optimize memory bandwidth utilization for irregular access patterns inherent in SpMV. The low-bit approximation in Stage 1 filters out irrelevant entries early, reducing the volume of full-precision computation dramatically.
